en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Longxiang Xiaoyin Yun:
Alas! This record has lain buried for over four hundred years, from the Yuan dynasty through the Ming, down to the present day.
Once it had come from nowhere, it suddenly emerged from the dragon palace and ocean treasury, falling into the hands of the Venerable Shanseng.

Shanseng, who held the seal of authority over Tiantong, saw this text pass through the hands of Ju and Li. It was encountered by the Elder Baifa, whose descendant, the Great Dharma Master Fanguang, presided over the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* and Tripitaka records at Zibai Monastery.
Because he regarded the ancestral life-force of the Buddhas and patriarchs as being of vital importance, [he preserved it].
Kuan. He specifically took up his staff and, together with the Daoist practitioners, swept through the monastery, inspecting and arranging everything.
Thereupon, he offered a fragrant incense ball and presented it to this record, suddenly causing the light of the thin bamboo slips to shine forth and shake the earth.

It was like the moment when the sword of Yanjin leaped from its scabbard or when the soil was wiped clean at Huayin—truly an inconceivable and most extraordinary cause and condition. Were it not for those who oversee and protect it, this would not have come to pass.

The staff of the mountain elder has now appeared before us. Master Xing’s life and karmic encounters are fully recorded in the *Record of the Practice of the Way* by Lord Yu, the Academician of the Quanzhang Pavilion, and in the *Epitaph for the Stupa* by Lord Huang, the Vice Director of the Imperial Library.
In brief, he received the Dharma from Master Xi of Mount Yangshan; as for the source of Xi’s lineage, it traces back to Dahui Zonggao.
Xī Lǎorén inherited the lineage from Fózhuàng Guāng; then Běijiàn Jiǎn, Wùchū Guān, and Huìméi Jī followed, and through them the lineage was transmitted to Xiàoyǐn.
Xiàoyǐn transmitted it to five disciples: Juéyuán Tánjì, Tántán, Lè, and others.
Only Juéyuán succeeded in transmitting it to Dìngyán Jiè, after which the lineage could no longer be traced. Consequently, Master Xīn’s *Púshì jí* (Pu-shi Collection) has circulated in the world.

The recorded sayings (*yulu*) from four assemblies—those at Wuhui in Huzhou, Baoguo in Hangzhou, Zhong Tianzhu, and finally Dajulongxiang in Jinling—which were previously granted entry into the canon, have instead fallen into obscurity and been lost to history.
This is because no one among his later followers has come forward to polish and preserve them.
Miaoxi encountered Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty and was twice appointed as abbot of Mount Jing by imperial decree; his school’s influence flourished greatly, and he was known at the time as...
Linji’s lineage was revived by Xiaoyin, who encountered Emperor Wen of the Yuan dynasty.

Following him from Jinling as he ascended the imperial throne, the Emperor established the Great Longxiang Jiqing Monastery at his former residence; he then summoned the Master to serve as its founding patriarch and invited him to the Northern Capital.

He was specially granted the third rank of the literary hierarchy (*wénjiē*) and appointed to preside over the Five Mountains of the Buddhist teachings. He was bestowed the title of Chan Master Guangzhì Quánwù.
While the monastic regulations traditionally required black robes, he was specially granted yellow robes; furthermore, his entire assembly of disciples were permitted to wear yellow robes as well.

The Master composed a poem regarding this initial change to yellow robes, which appears in the *Pǔshí jí* (Pu-shi Collection), stating: "Returning from receiving my decree before the Xuānzhào Pavilion, I have been newly granted the imperial yellow."
The entire city took notice. I, this monk, recall the days when I was a śrāmaṇera; we all donned green robes and ascended the ordination platform.

On that day, while residing in a new monastery to the south, I was summoned to the imperial court in the north. I was treated with exceptional courtesy and honored with high praise; the gifts bestowed upon me were beyond measure.

For a time, the glory of the National Teacher shone forth, and such an extraordinary event for the Buddha-dharma was rare even in a thousand years. Looking back at the two imperial edicts issued to Jing Mountain by Miaoxi, these [current honors] are even more prominent than a banner on a staff.
This is a step forward. Read Master Xun’s Complete Record with diligence! Ten thousand phenomena manifest together, yet not a single speck of dust intrudes.

With the sinews of the eyes and the bones of the tongue, he causes a thunderous resonance throughout all quarters. Such great capacity and great function can truly kick over Mount Sumeru and overturn the vast ocean.
Above me is Great Wisdom (Mahāmati), and simultaneously there is Zhongfeng; their understanding enters the boundless, so that we may perhaps race side by side and vie for precedence.
Since I, the Daoist Sweeper, took refuge in the Patriarch Han from Caoxi, I have encountered all the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) of the various quarters face-to-face.
Having studied the *Rujian Chan Tongqi*, I have gained some knowledge of how to investigate the mind. Consequently, I reflect upon the saying of "one flower and five petals."
Thus, the lineages of the Five Houses and Five Lamps were established. Of these, the two houses of Guiyang and Linji originated from Nanyue;
the three houses of Yunmen, Fayan, Caodong, and Linji originated from Qingyuan.

While the Guiyang, Yunmen, and Fayan schools were like the *utpala* flower, appearing once and then vanishing, only the two lamps of Linji and Caodong have burned with a constant flame, as recorded in the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*.
Regarding the lineages of Dharma succession recorded in various texts such as the *Wudeng Huiyuan*, the *Zhengfa Zhengzong Ji*, the *Sengbao Zhuan*, the *Zhiyue Lu*, and the *Fozu Gangjian*:

although these exist within them, there are instances where some individuals lived for many years while others were short-lived, or where some were born late yet lived long while others were born young and died early.

These accounts are inconsistent and prone to confusion, making it difficult to verify them. Furthermore, the surnames and names of the two families (the patriarchal and maternal lines) are frequently subject to ambiguity, error, and corruption. Upon examination...
Throughout the annals of successive dynasties, the records of our presence and disappearance are vast and obscure.
During the eras of emperors such as Zhou Wu, Tang Wu, and Song Hui, who venerated the Way (Daoism) and suppressed Buddhism, the Dharma was diminished and the transmission of its lamp grew dark.

Yet, during the flourishing periods of the early Tang, early Song, and early Ming dynasties, when the Dharma was propagated through translation and circulation, the teachings were at their peak while the core vehicle (the *zong*) of the lineage, conversely, declined. At those times, was it not for want of worthy individuals?

The records of the patriarchs’ transmissions all reside within the interstices of concealment and manifestation, appearance and disappearance. There is no basis for manifestly sealing this Buddha-dharma;

rather, it is due to the seasonal causes and conditions that it was entrusted to kings and great ministers. Master Dàchuān Hóng made the *Wǔdēng Huìyuán* (The Five Lamps Compiled), yet from the time Míxi opened the Dharma onwards, his compilation was muddled.
He simply stated: "From the time of Emperor Xiào Zōng of the Sòng dynasty onwards, [the lineage of] the masters who transmitted the Dharma..."

For five hundred years, both [theories] have remained beyond verification. In the early Ming dynasty, Shen Shirong of Jian’an composed the *Continuation of the Discourse on the Original Teaching* (*Xu Yuanjiao lun*), stating directly:
"Since Master Zhongfeng withdrew from his seat, we have not known where the Way has been hidden. Fortunately, the teachings still possess clear texts that serve as witnesses for the mind;
the life of wisdom has not yet been severed, though it hangs like a single thread. Both discourses are currently included in the Tripitaka and are indeed authentic.
This is what is meant. One must know that within this, there is but a single point which distinguishes the true from the false.
As for their differences, even within a single school there are distinctions between the formal arrangements of the gate and the courtyard;
yet as for their commonality, beyond two schools there is no difference in the secret transmission of the lineage. Taking a single school as an example, such as Linji: by means of...
The Three Sages constitute the direct lineage; this is the transmission from the Three Sages through which Huizhao re-established the Dharma.
Fuguo took Dahui as his direct successor; this is the transmission from Dahui through Hujing. Dongshan took Caoshan as his direct successor; this is the transmission from Caoshan through Yunju.
Since these two lineages were transmitted side by side, it is difficult to distinguish between the collateral and the primary. Judging by these two schools:
For example, Xuefeng went up to Dongshan nine times and ascended Touzi three times, yet he ultimately succeeded Deshan;

this is Dong [Lin] following Ji [Xuan]. Danxia personally received the seal of approval from Mazu, yet he ultimately succeeded Shitou; this is Ji [Xuan] following Dong [Lin]. These two lineages were transmitted interchangeably, making it difficult to distinguish guest from host.
When one’s wisdom surpasses that of the teacher, what need is there for further exhortation? When demons and heretics are cowed into submission, what need is there for...
Do not engage in contentious disputes. The Venerable Miaoxi praised himself, saying: "It is like transforming a kunpeng;
it simply transforms itself—how could there be any dharma? Xiaoyin also raised his voice against Heiji, saying: "Within a peach pit a thousand years old, what 'kernel' from the past can you seek?
These are the very words from beyond the age of Wei-yin; they are the true seed of the One Flower and Five Leaves. It should be...
At this time of vast upheaval when mountains become valleys and the void itself perishes, there appears a master such as the Venerable Shanseng,
who, with a universal mind, a great mind, and a boundless vision, ceases searching for flowers, leaves, roots, and stems, and instead disregards the tangled vines and branches,
allowing all worldly entanglements to vanish entirely. Like Master Xun’s record here, it is as if cold ashes suddenly burst into flame and blood splashes against the Brahma Heaven.
How could this possibly be mentioned in the same breath as those who fill the void of space? Moved by these thoughts, I set down my brush and sighed three times.

On the full moon of the twelfth month of the year Wushen (1656) of the Shunzhi era, by Yu, former Jiaermen (second rank) jinshi of the Wuchen year, currently serving as Director of the National Academy.
Compiled by the Court Official Fu, Disciple of Caoxi Fuzheng, Layman Li Dao-yi,
Sa’ān Tan Zhenmo, and Pan Tan;
*The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xiyin Yun*, Volume One.
Recorded at Wuhui Chan Temple in Huzhou Prefecture,
compiled by the disciples Tingjun and others.
On the first day of the eighth month in the fourth year of Zhida, the Master composed this at Jingci Chan Temple in Hangzhou Prefecture.
Having recorded the invitation from the administrative quarters, he entered the monastery and ascended the hall, saying:
"The flower was plucked and the Dharma entrusted; facing the wall, the mind was settled. Schools were established and lineages divided, yet they have only served to obstruct one another.
[Holding up his staff and drawing a line]—with this single stroke, everything is cut off. We may rejoice that all under heaven is at peace. And so it is..."

The soldiers follow the turning of the seal; the generals pursue the movement of the talisman. When a new elder appears in the world to act as a man for others, what matter does he ultimately clarify?
Have you not seen how when Baoshou opened the hall, Sansheng pushed forward a monk, and Baoshou immediately struck him?
Sansheng said, "If you act as a teacher in this manner, you will not only blind the eyes of this monk, but you will go on to blind the people of the entire city of Zhenzhou."
Baoshou cast down his staff and returned to the abbot’s quarters. Cutting through like a chisel through iron, he manifested the true mechanism beyond the ordinary;
gathering and releasing at will, he displayed the orthodox eye of the present moment. Truly, dragons howled as mist rose and tigers roared as winds sprang up;
a single ray of divine light pierced through past and present. Even such a proclamation still involves the journey—how much more so to speak of arriving home and sitting securely.
"How do you express this in a single phrase? "The three robes and the monk's staff beyond the green peaks; A single burner of aloeswood incense amidst the white clouds.
He ascended the hall and said: "If I press my finger, the Ocean Seal manifests first. You all, throughout the twelve periods of the day—whether turning, moving, bowing, or rising;
whether ascending to your beds, descending to the ground, opening your mats, or unfolding your bowls—it is not that the Ocean Seal does not radiate light. Day is bright and night is dark; summer..."
The coming of winter and the passing of spring; the crows cawing and the magpies chirping; the wind stirring and the dust rising—these are not the radiance of the Sea-Seal (Haiyin).
Cloud Gate’s (Yunmen) "sesame cake" and Zhaozhou’s “tea” are not the radiance of the Sea-Seal. Xuefeng’s rolling the ball and Niu-tou’s dancing are not the radiance of the Sea-Seal. Some might say:
"The wisdom of all-knowledge is pure, for it is non-dual, without division, without distinction, and without interruption. This too is not so.
This is washing soil with mud. Ultimately, how is it? The soil-dweller has much beard and mustache under his chin; the Persian from the South Sea has large nostrils.
Entering the hall: Driving the plowman’s ox, seizing the hungry man’s food—clucking and pecking at the same moment, arrow-points meeting directly. A single punch!
A punch returns a punch; a kick returns a kick. Ox-head to the south, horse-head to the north.
Entering the summer retreat, he ascends the hall; at Bóyán, they open the gruel for the summer retreat. At Xīyuàn, they deliberate on two errors. The Great Elephant of Jiāzhōu treads upon the earth;
the Iron Ox of Shǎnfǔ wears horns upon its head. (He lets out a shout. One must strictly avoid binding oneself without a rope.
Ascending the hall at the Green Sprouts Assembly: On this auspicious morning, I respectfully wish that the Head Seat and the great assembly may enjoy abundant blessings.

For these past few days, we have prayed for the protection of the green sprouts and troubled you with the chanting of sutras. That wind and rain come in their proper seasons is the Way of Heaven; that the hundred grains grow and mature is the benefit of the Earth.
Thus, the Patriarch said: "The ground of the mind gives birth to all seeds; through phenomena, one returns to the principle. When the fruit is full..."
The Bodhi-maṇḍala: the world arises as flowers bloom. [He suddenly picks up his staff and says:

"This staff has traveled to the Western Heavens and is now returning to the land of Silla. [He strikes the ground once and says: "A stone ox blocks the ancient road; one horse gives birth to three tigers."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the example of Zen Master Xiangyan, who addressed the assembly, saying: "It is like a man climbing a tree, holding a branch in his mouth, with his hands not grasping branches and his feet not treading on the trunk.
If someone beneath the tree asks about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, to answer would mean losing one's life;
not to answer would mean failing the questioner. At such a moment, what is to be done? At that time, there was Houtou...
Zuochu said, "I do not ask about [the master] having climbed the tree; I request the Master to speak before he has climbed it.
Xiangyan laughed heartily. The Master composed a verse: "Each time he lifts it up, he furrows his brow; How is climbing the tree compared to not yet having climbed?
Who is there in the painted tower on a bright moonlit night, Holding a jade flute upside down, blowing into the wind?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "The sense bases and their objects are unimpeded; things and self are one and the same. A needle-eyed fish sucks dry the four great oceans; a gnat swallows Mount Sumeru.
Why is it that the person within the hermitage does not know what is outside the hermitage?
After a long silence, he said: "Maitreya drags a cloth bag through the streets; Zhaozhou hangs a gourd on the wall."
Ascending the hall, Master Huanglong Nan said: "To speak of the wondrous and the profound is to be a traitor in times of peace;
to wield the staff and shout is to be a hero in times of chaos. Therefore, as for the two words 'Buddha-dharma,' I have never once uttered them."
Nevertheless, everyone must know this. Holding up his staff, he said: "In Zhenzhou they grow large radishes;
at White’s house in Qingyuan there are three cups of wine. When guests arrive, serve them according to what is available. When meeting others, there is no need to air one's family's private faults."
Holding his staff, he descended from the seat and ascended the hall, saying:
"On the long meditation benches you grasp your nostrils; on the crossroads of the street you lose your eyes.
Have you all ever examined this yet? It is as bright as the sun, yet as black as lacquer. At the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, one lets go and walks forth."
The "True Person of No Rank" is stark naked.

Entering the hall, he cited the case of Deshan arriving at Guishan, where he carried his bundle up to the Dharma Hall, walking from east to west and from west to east, looking around and saying, "Nothing, nothing," and then departed.
Upon reaching the gate, he spoke again: "One must not be hasty. Then [he]—
Maintaining his dignified demeanor, Deshan entered again for an audience. Holding up his sitting mat, he called out, "Preceptor!
As Guishan reached for his whisk, Deshan let out a shout, shook out his sleeves, and departed. That evening, Guishan asked the Head Seat, "Where did that newcomer go just now?
The Head Seat replied, "At that moment, he turned his back on the Dharma Hall and went off wearing straw sandals."
Guishan said, "This fellow will hereafter go to the summit of a solitary peak, build a thatched hut, and proceed to revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs.
The Master composed a verse on this: Striding alone through the vast expanse, turning left and right; The golden crow beats its wings, and the waves of the sea surge.
An iron net hangs upside down over coral trees; the horizontal mechanism is silent and vast, and the myriad phenomena sink into stillness.
Fully killing and fully giving life, able to release and able to capture—do not begrudge the lack of strength in this old man; amidst a mere laugh and jest, the brocade trap is deep.
Ascending the hall, he brandished his hammer and held up his whisk. To press one's eyes is to see flowers; to cite the ancients and discuss the present is to drive a wedge into empty space.
Master Yangqi said, "Mount Sumeru can be pierced through, but the Diamond Circle cannot be pierced through. The great ocean can be swallowed, but the thorny *liji* fruit cannot be swallowed.
Even if you could swallow it and pierce through it, that is still not the business of a patch-robed monk. How so?
This is the business of the patch-robed monk. Return to the hall and go for tea. Opening the furnace, I ascend the hall:
dwelling in this monastery, I am ashamed to lack merit; winter has come, yet there is nothing at all. My house is poor and I am too shy to see guests;

charcoal is scarce and the furnace has not yet been lit. The walls are broken and need more mud to patch them; the windows are drafty and lack paper to plaster them. There is no patriarchal intent in the West—let us examine it!
Poh-lao-hu ascended the hall and said:
"The World-Honored One was once at the assembly on Vulture Peak. There was a woman who sat near the Buddha and entered into samādhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: 'Why is it that this woman is permitted to sit near the Buddha while I am not? The Buddha replied:"
"You need only awaken this woman and cause her to rise from samādhi; you may ask her yourself.

Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times and snapped his fingers once, even extending [his power] up to the Brahma Heaven; yet, despite exhausting all his supernatural powers, he could not bring her out.
The Buddha said, "Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs, they could not bring this woman out of her meditative concentration. Below [this world], beyond forty-two..."
"In lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti who can bring this woman out of her samādhi.
Immediately, Vimalakīrti surged forth from the earth before the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One commanded Vimalakīrti to bring the woman out of her samādhi.
Vimalakīrti snapped his fingers once before the woman, and she thereupon emerged from her samādhi. The Master raised his whisk and struck it down.
Zhaozhou said, "A single string has pierced them all.
He ascended the hall and said: "A tattered blue robe is buffeted by the north wind; Dust on the face, ash on the head, and tears filling the beard.

The place where he stood in the snow at Shaolin to seek the Dharma, The time when he ceased his studies for fear of the cold at the Fen River. The rocky cliffs crumble, destroying the mountain’s bones; The icy ravines are jagged and steep."
The earth’s surface cracks and splits open; the Dharma-body is startled awake, finding no place to cling. Riding backward upon an iron horse, he ascends Mount Sumeru.
Compiled by the disciples Huitan and others from the *Recorded Sayings* of the Chan Master of Baoguo Temple on the Road to Hangzhou.
On the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Yanyou era, he entered the temple.
Opening the hall, he held up the incense and said:

"This incense is burned toward the precious burner specifically to pray for the longevity of the present Emperor—ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years. Next, holding up the incense, he said: "This incense is offered..."

For the officials of the Xuanzheng Yuan dispatched by the Zhongshu Sheng for the circuit of Zhejiang and other regions, as well as the civil and military officials of all departments, I offer this incense to augment their life-span and merit.
Again, he holds up the incense and says: "This incense was once realized beneath a single phrase on the summit of Mount Daxiong;
today it is offered before the fivefold assembly at Mount Fenghuang. It is respectfully offered on behalf of the former abbot of Jing..."
Later, he resided at Dayang. To repay the grace of the Dharma-milk, the Great Monk Huiji, the Zen Master Fozhi, took his seat.
After the exchange of questions and answers was concluded, he said: "To gaze into the clouds from the summit of a solitary peak—would this not be burying one's own spiritual brilliance?
To mix mud and water in the middle of the crossroads—this is what is valued for the circulation of the true eye. He raised his staff and said: "Śākya..."

Kāśyapa has already passed away and Maitreya is not yet born; it is precisely this very day. The life-vein of the thousand sages and the tongs and hammer of the successive patriarchs are all now in the hands of the National Master Xinbao.
When he lifts them up, they are pierced through in every direction; at every turn, the boundless wondrous body manifests.

Letting go, it mirrors the earth and illuminates the heavens; everywhere, the precious king’s ocean of lands is revealed. What need is there to say that "streams and mountains differ, yet clouds and moon are the same"?
The ultimate transformation is effortless, its function without a master; vast and open, it is a single expanse of the ancient sovereign’s wind.
Again, he cited Master Zhi, who sent someone to deliver a message to Dayi (Sida), saying: "Why do you not go down the mountain to teach and transform sentient beings?
What is the point of looking up at the Milky Way all the time? Dayi replied: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time have been swallowed by me in a single gulp;
where else could there be any sentient beings to be saved? The Master said: "Once pressed by Master Zhi, Dayi was driven straight [to his realization]."
One may retreat three thousand steps.

Whether advancing or retreating, the two orders ascend the hall; with a mind empty, one attains the highest degree. Why must one select an official when selecting a Buddha? To shoulder the burden of the monastic groves.

To act for the sake of the multitude is just as if acting for oneself; to repay the nation and serve the Dharma is to select people according to their capacity and assign offices based on their talent. It is like a musical performance of the nine-fold *jiǔchéng*:

whether advancing or retreating, every movement conforms to the measure. Consider this: when a single shout distinguishes guest from host, and the functions of illumination and application are exercised simultaneously—how do you all discern this?
(He lets out a shout. When the nine-tenthousand-li Peng bird first unfurls its wings, the three-thousand...
The crane of a hundred years then soared away.
[The Master] ascended the hall and raised the following: Master Nanyuan Huanglong, while in his quarters, posed this koan:

"What is my hand like a Buddha’s hand? What is my foot like a donkey’s foot? Every person has their own karmic affinity from birth; which one is the senior monk’s affinity from birth? The Master said:
Huanglong’s Three Barriers were like Shangjun’s establishment of laws; though the laws were implemented, they discarded the Way of the former kings.
Consequently, while many emerged from his school at that time, those who truly received his transmission became increasingly few.
Had he strictly adhered to the family precepts of Ciming, his descendants would not have been brought to such an end.
One day the Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "I have come from traveling the mountains.

The Master said, "As for that which was used by Luopu during his travels when he pressed down under his straw hat—how is it now? The monk said, "Even before entering this gate, I have already presented it to the Master.
The Master said, "Why do you not bring it forth right now? The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him.
Ascending the Dharma Hall on the Anniversary of the Sage’s Birthday: Descending from Tuṣita to Jambudvīpa, his fundamental essence and manifested traces are non-dual;

governing the golden wheel, he proclaims the True Dharma, wherein the provisional and the real are fully revealed. Riding upon his vows, he manifests birth; according to capacities, he unfolds transformation. The spiritual pivot moves in secret, elevating our people to the midst of Anāgata-sukhāvatī;
the precious mirror is held high, placing the four seas within the crucible of the Great Potter. Therefore, we of this forest and spring...

Beneath this, the days of transformation lengthen; amidst the clarity of the bells and drums, the profound wind spreads afar. The three wheels do not abide, and both giver and receiver are relinquished.
Ultimately, how should one offer praise? After a long silence, he said: "The merit of non-action is inconceivable;
the pure wisdom of the wondrous, perfect body is empty and quiescent."

Ascending the hall at the conclusion of the summer retreat: Zen practitioners, as you depart east and west at the end of the summer, do not merely say you are carrying your packs to catch the early cool.
The three realms are blazing like a house on fire; who knows where one’s true hometown lies?
Ascending the hall: In the middle month of the eighth lunar month, the sun and moon are being eroded away. When will the clear-eyed monk discern the mark?
The great earth, mountains, and rivers—light and dark, penetration and obstruction—are fundamentally pure; the vast void leaves no trace. Manjushri’s wisdom enters infinite bodies;
Avalokiteshvara’s compassion responds in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Within a single hair-tip lie hundreds of thousands of samadhis; go ask them upon the long meditation benches.
To the distinguished guests:
On the Mid-Autumn Day, the Master ascended the hall and cited Panshan’s saying: “The mind-moon is solitary and full; its light swallows the ten thousand phenomena.
The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist. When both light and objects have vanished, what is it? The Master said, “Panshan has a fine ‘mind-moon.’”
A solitary circle. Furthermore, what thing is this path? It is a pity that the words have been split into two fragments.
To serve one’s country is not to take official property for one's own personal favor; it is also to ensure that all people may enjoy it together. Jade dew falls silently upon the shadowless tree;
the golden wind stirs slightly at the night-bright curtain. The wooden man whips up the earthen ox, which bellows; the azure dragon is not permitted to lie down.
At Bitan, he ascended the hall and said: "Words uttered are not sounds; forms presented are not objects. What is the reason for this attachment?

To sleep within sound and form, to sit and lie down within sound and form—this is already somewhat better. Therefore it is said: 'This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing; there is nothing else.'"

"Sound and form may be presented before you; if you understand this very point, there is fundamentally nothing to do. What harm is there in distinguishing or not distinguishing between essence and function?

He suddenly picked up his staff and said, "Where does the flowing water and yellow leaf come from? An ox with a cold crow passes through another village. He struck the ground with the staff and descended from the seat.
One day the Master said: "If you step once upon the crown of my head, the worlds of the ten directions will crumble like ice melting away.
Where, then, shall you all meet with this mountain monk?"
A monk was standing in attendance. The Master spread out both hands and said, "It has been opened wide like the eight characters;
why do you not accept it? The monk said, "I fear only that I would be making a fool of the Master. The Master said, "For so long you have lacked even a single breath of life," and he struck him.
On New Year’s Eve, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Living in the city at year's end is like being in a deep village; The ancient monk’s way of life preserves the Way itself.
The mud ox from the bottom of the sea plows the azure void; The straw dog in the clouds barks at twilight. Every dust mote contains and encompasses the three thousand worlds."

The Dharma-dharmas are perfectly fulfilled in the Gate of Non-duality; they are left entirely to the four seasons like the turning of a wheel hub. One must know that heaven and earth share the same root.

[He] ascended the hall and, citing the question posed by Zhimen to Master Wuzu Ji, said: "I do not ask about the passing of spring and the arrival of winter; rather, regarding those beneath the forest..."
"How is it when we meet? Jie said, "Listening to the jade water-clock before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion. Men said, "What can be done? The Main Mountain is high and the Forehead Mountain is low.
Jie said, "Striking the golden bell atop the summit of Mount Sumeru. The Master composed a verse: "The rabbit and the horse have horns."

The ox and the sheep have no horns; they are utterly hairless and utterly wool-less. Like mountains and like peaks, at the Ox-Islet they are as sharp as rhinoceros horns, parting the waves and billows of the ocean floor.
At Yanping, the swords unite, dispersing into rain and hail across the clear sky. How vast!
Across the river, a beckoning hand reaches out to one who knows the music—what need is there to wait for the awakening after a single night at Caoxi?

The statue of the Abbot of Chongde Temple in Wuxi stands firm like gathered clouds;
with its solemnity, it soars like a phoenix. Possessing the lofty spirit of a secluded valley and the magnanimity of the Five Lakes, he remained there without ever venturing abroad.

Yet when dragon-elephants come to visit, they do not engage in formal social courtesies, and renowned gentlemen still yearn for them like ants. This may be compared to a cold spring or an ancient well, whose flavor becomes ever sweeter;
or like jade in the mountains, whose brilliance shines forth from without. I have not personally seen your portrait on silk, Master Zhan, yet its splendor is already manifest.
When shall we share a smile beneath a rain of flowers? I listen intently as your eloquence pours forth like the cascade of the Silver River.

Though the elder brother in the Dharma, the late Master Xiangyan, was as precious as a jade *hu* or *lian* vessel, he was not as valuable as the uncut gem from Mount Jing; though one may serve as a ridgepole or a beam, it is not as noble as the reclining of the ancient pines.
Therefore, Zhongling and Juefan, in guiding their disciples, lacked the ten thousand fingers and the thousand foundations required to bear heavy burdens and travel far;

they were like the rivers and seas compared to the mountains and peaks, or like my own *tāixū* (Great Void) surpassing them. Yet, in contending with these two elders, when the bamboo whisk struck back or touched, it scattered white rain from the clear sky;
the Vajra-jewel sword roared like thunder at the door of the hibernating insects. Just as one was about to don his robes—
He obtained the seat; in an instant, he lay down firmly and closed the door. I gazed up at him from afar, waiting for the assembly.
"The lineage of my late master is as cold as ice; I must follow the example of the old masters Yangqi and Jiufeng, pulling the plow and dragging the harrow through this life."
The portrait of the late Master Donglu of Yong’an in Fuzhou: his noble bearing was vast and profound;

his spontaneous wit was unimpeded. He was the direct successor of Zhongfeng, whose melodic voice reached its full perfection after nine performances; he was the one who upheld the legacy of the Southern School.
A rare unicorn with a single horn, he has received the imperial decree with honor; his fame illuminates the mountains and rivers of his native village.
Seated in eternal peace, he conjures the pavilions and towers of the Five Indias. With the Vajra sword brandished before him, who is the true connoisseur but Zhang Tianjue?
His gaze is like the moon, his snow-white brows are deep; a chilling pure wind stirs the hills and valleys.
Sengqitai painted an image of his master, Rashipaba, and requested a eulogy.

His voice reached the Five Indias; his lineage originated from Xiliang. He was foretold in the secret records of the Superior Master (Atiśa). He dyed his robes vermilion, imbuing them with the fragrance of the Nine Heavens.
Holding mantras, he subdued demons, transmitting the secrets of Amoghavajra. Shaking his bell as he entered the marketplace, he emulated the deeds of Puhua.
Feigning madness, he harmonized the ultimate and the conventional, emptying all existence. His lineage flows on in succession, the dharma-lineage long and flourishing.
At Zangshan Temple, the Elder Fulu’s image caused sweet spring water to gush forth from the earth;
yet this was not as practical as rice and grain. When the heavens hang auspicious clouds, how can they compare to the nourishing rain and dew?
Moistening and nourishing all, the Master focused on the fundamental and did not seek the peripheral; he investigated the reality and did not dally with mere rhetoric.

He cultivated the Pure Land with comprehensive practice, uniquely capturing the essential intent of Yongming; when his golden gong resounded once, the mechanism of universal transformation was re-illuminated.

The myriad phenomena and the vast cosmos listened to his commands, and the ancestral Way of a thousand years relied upon his guidance. Let us cease discussing the "Huanzhu" (Abiding in Illusion) school.
Bark and marrow; I bow my head to the foremost branch of the *udumbara*.
This is the portrait of the Great Master Tongzhi of Lingfeng Temple on the Riverbank. His disciple, the Head Seat Xuanshou, requested a eulogy.
To seek jade, one visits Mount Jing; to seek timber, one enters the Deng Forest. Of our school, the *udumbara* flower shines brilliantly upon the azure cloud peaks.
From the Yuquan school emerged Nanquan; like a hundred streams converging into the sea. From the land of Zhushan, the mind was transmitted to the Eastern Land;
like melting various vessels into a single piece of gold. The divine sword undergoes transformations—vainly one gazes toward the energy of the Dipper and Ox stars.
The numinous rhinoceros horn appears and disappears—who can fathom the depth of the vast blue sea? Alas! This man has passed away; my heart labors in vain. [The circle]
The sound of the "Snow in the Chamber" melody ought to be heard; with such lofty tones, who could harmonize with this zither whose strings have vanished?
To this day, by the clear waters of the river at the sacred stupa, the wind and rain are occasionally heard to intone like the dragon’s cry.
I trust that the image from the South Sea (Ssufozhi) speaks of "blind" Chan;
having attained teacherless wisdom, he understands how to employ Linji’s “white-pickpocketing” and is adept at using Nanshan’s “tortoise-nose.”
It was simply because, while traveling on foot, I failed to meet the right person. I misunderstood Baizhang’s words as he descended from the hall.

From that time on, returning to the summit of Dayu Ridge, we have called out to one another and dragged each other down into demonic delusions. Born of the same lineage, yet dying of different lineages—who among us is the elder brother or the younger?
There are disciples who paint my likeness and bow before me; their karmic grievances from past lives leave no room for evasion. One should regard them as a clay owl.
I shall destroy the pack of man-eating demons, ransack their lairs, and exterminate their kind; after thirty years, I will vent my wrath upon you.

You who have received the teachings from the founding patriarch of Suiluo Temple—whose image shows fangs like tigers and eyes like lightning, with thick brows and a withered neck—you who uphold the traditions of Dongsi and the lineage of Zhaozhou, clear away the rubble and debris!
He served as the abbot of Yama Palace. He sat at the critical ford upon the Western River.

As for his family dharma not falling into decline, there was Baiyun, who received instruction from Chaling; and there was Fotang, whose hall emitted light, who studied together with Guling under Baizhang.
I offer praise and hymns; my tongue falters as words fail me. Gazing beyond the heavens for divine radiance, may your lifespan be equal to that of empty space.
Your descendants shall be numerous, many as dragon elephants.
Portrait of Master Guishan of Tianchi.

His disciple, Attendant Mao, requested a eulogy for one of complete virtue who does not begrudge his weight when holding high office, nor seek to conform to the tastes of the age when transmitting the Way.
In antiquity there was such a man: Fengxue and Yangqi, who fully bore the lineage of Linji, as precarious as nine tripods suspended by a single thread—truly magnificent!
Ah, Master Shansheng! Your conduct is not ashamed before the ancients; you are the true successor of Yuanying and the compass for later students.
For forty years you sat at Tianchi, where none of those who came in twos, threes, fours, or sevens were your fellow practitioners. Ten thousand points of celestial lamps arrive in the deep night.
In vain did I promise to engage in discourse with Mañjuśrī.
Elder Huizhi painted the Master’s portrait;

I was requested to compose a eulogy for the wondrous words of the Dharma of the mind, yet they cannot be fully proclaimed. When the Great Function manifests, there is nothing of the mind to be transmitted. Thus, Yongjia said:

Upon arriving at Caoxi, Zhaozhou met Nanquan; their spiritual resonance responded spontaneously, their divine radiance perfectly round—like water flowing over the earth, like the sun traversing the heavens.
He unleashed the "tortoise-nosed" staff from the South Mountain, leaving heaven and earth devoid of color, and startled the carp of the Eastern Sea into leaping forth.

Wind and rain sweep across the eight extremities of the world; the Zen school feels ashamed that I am merely filling its vacancy. I alone steer this hundred-leak boat—its hide is pierced through and its bones are exposed, with half of its nostrils left as hollows.
On the Lan River, I recall our past together listening to the monkeys on Lotus Peak.

When shall we vent our long-held grievances? With poisonous hands and aged fists, I shall strike back. Is what I have depicted in these brushstrokes similar to the reality? Upon the Yichun Terrace, the moon shines with exquisite clarity.

The Venerable Baoshan Qu requested a eulogy for Baizhang’s “one shout that deafened for three days” and Linji’s “sixty-year-old willow branch whisk. I have no single dharma to show those who come to study;
I am ashamed, my mouth like a wooden stump. There is no need to present the Buddha’s hand or the donkey’s feet; the faces of the sun and moon are this.
What thing is this? Without cause, it is held toward the Hall of the Treasure Mountain. Wind and thunder shake the Dragon Cave.
Elder Qingquan Hai requests a eulogy for the transmission outside the golden robe.
The monastery pole is overturned; the ancestral livelihood is shattered and the family line is broken. The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.

"Extinguished at the side of the blind donkey; sealed with a single seal. The tiger’s body was originally striped. Taking up Zhaozhou’s seven-pound robe, the collar is lifted and the elbow is revealed.
Handling Dongshan’s three blows of the staff, the teeth are clenched and the gums are pierced.
Now it is entrusted to Nanquan, who causes the eighteen rapids of the West River to surge."

The Elder Fu requested a verse to praise Baizhang’s mistaken response to a turning phrase. Deshan did not understand the "final word," and as it was transmitted to later generations, it became increasingly distorted.
One seeks to plant a tree of no form within the fire; the decrepit Dragon River has no root upon which to rely. A black hen amidst the snow.
Having once again received this pointed instruction, it is entrusted to Changning: simply proceed in this manner. The Lion of West River naturally transcends the crowd;
the Qilin on the celestial shore is seen to stride alone.

The Elder Banyue requested a eulogy, yet he does not recognize characters, does not practice Chan, and is uniformly crude—mistaking north for south. Failing to understand the final word, he erroneously misidentifies the "threes and threes" from the beginning.
I may privately compare him to the old master Shimen; how could he succeed Yun’an? His lofty spirit is difficult to conceive, and I am filled with concern.

Our shared afflictions are as familiar as they are common; mere brushstrokes and pigments can only vainly attempt to capture them. As we gaze upon one another, it becomes increasingly unbearable. I vow to thatch a hut for the end of the year, when yellow leaves shall fill the thousand crags.
*Written at the request of the Elder Nanchan Yu.*

Regarding the three types of leadership in the monastic groves—preaching the Dharma, providing for the assembly, and maintaining the monastery—I have resided on this mountain for over thirty years, yet upon inspection, I find myself deficient in every single one.
I am unable to support the teachings through my reading, nor can I transmit the Way through Zen meditation.
I know only how to scold, revile, and shout; I am nothing but stubborn and irritable by nature. It was Xinghua who drove out Kebin, and Mazu who kicked down Shuilao.
Were it not for a false, cruel, and biting pair of tongs and a hammer, how could one be called a "grass of our own house"?
To ensure that these words spread far and wide, they are entrusted to the Elder Nanchan.
Elder Liang of Zisheng requests a eulogy.

Narrow-minded and impetuous, he appeared violent; straightforward and candid, he seemed arrogant. Wherever he went, he encountered slander and censure; he maintained few friendships with the common world.

He resided in official monasteries according to circumstance, feeling ashamed of empty honors and bestowed titles. He did not penetrate the Chan of Linji, merely waving his arms and sweeping wildly about.

He split apart the three mysteries and the essentials, yet neither word nor meaning reached them. He could not distinguish between illumination and function; master and guest were mutually inverted. Zisheng...
Having long followed one another, we have been permitted to penetrate deeply into the profound gate. There is this "final phrase" which, in the end, will never be directed toward the common path.
Only when the Eye of the True Dharma is extinguished can one truly be called a "kitchen-stealer."
A Verse to See Off Master Xing of Wuning as He Returns to Mount Lu to Resume His Studies:

The rushing green waters pour for six hundred li; Cloud-patterned brocade unrolls in the clear light across nine tiers of screens. In both the seizing of the landscape and the seizing of the person, neither prevails.
Setting out, the boy at the gate smiled as he welcomed them.

The two venerable masters, Xuánlì and Èrshàng, had thoroughly penetrated the profound mysteries of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of Mount Jìngshān. With eyes upon their staffs, do not hasten too much; pack your bags and go forth without a thousand [doubts].
In this village, one must meet the eighty-year-old elder Lingxiao;
inquire after the National Teacher of the Southeast. With the eyes and hands of his entire body, he distinguishes the kin from the stranger;
a single, perfect phrase shatters all into fragments—a speck of dust at the bottom of the well, a fish upon the mountain.
Seeing Off Elder Gu-yu’s Return to Guangxi by Imperial Decree:
The fragrance of heaven fills his coarse robe; atop Ma-wang Pavilion, he watches the clouds fly.
Had he known early that the mountain is the very body of Suchness (Tathatā), why wait until seeking it on the sea before returning home?

I have long suffered in my efforts to welcome you and grew weary of dwelling in the mountains. Now that Your Majesty has preached the Dharma and moved the heart of the Dragon, you shall surely open the realm of longevity for those in the remote frontiers.
Thus, I shall return ten thousand *li* once more to the land between the Elephant and the Cinnamon Trees.
A Gift to Attendant Yanyan of Tiantong:
"You owe me, and I owe you. Where it curves like a hook, it is straight as a string. The waters of the Ning River flow swiftly eastward;
Mount Taibai is so high it does not touch the heavens."
We once dwelt together amidst the mountains of India; we have met again beneath the city walls of Shitou.
A net woven from tortoise hair spreads across the heavens—what can even the phoenixes soaring to the sky do against it?
The worthy attendant entered Zhejiang;

there was something to say, so I need not trouble myself copying it on paper. The maple leaves in the Imperial Garden are just right for writing upon. Where has Longxiang gone that we should be forsaken?
With a single oar against the west wind, I enter Wu once more.
Sending off the Master of Men, Dharma Master Zhi:
upright and straightforward, without artifice or hypocrisy. When hot, he seeks cool; when hungry, he eats.
With the eight characters fully opened, nothing can penetrate them. Three before and three after.

As I send off Master Yuan, walking, sitting, and lying down are all in accordance with conditions; throughout daily life, how has he ever strayed into the biased or the correct? On the branchless tree, the wind roars;
beyond the curtain of night-brightness, the moon is exquisite.

Supreme bliss is enjoyed within one's own home as the constant samādhi; whether moving against or with the current, or traversing in any direction, it is fundamentally spontaneous. The vast, swirling red dust is the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī);
the blazing mass of fire is the Heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna.
Presented to the Elder Wugai of Hainan:
Long have I heard of the Jade Bureau’s return to Danyang; I still remember the Dragon’s hidden majesty.
Nine thousand li across the vermilion cliffs and azure seas— A single staff, like drifting clouds, flies at will.
The Venerable Qi has returned to Hainan, while Master Song resides by the river in Tanchuan. A memorial was submitted to the Gate of the Azure Void, and the five clouds parted;
at night, the six tortoises bore away the divine mountain, yet still there is a monk coming from the South Sea.
The Moon-Treasury Master returns from seclusion to rearrange the Great Canon;
this is a matter of great urgency. Ultimately, who can recognize the authentic text?
At the Thousand-Year Cliff, tonight’s moon and the vermilion cassia trees fall in profusion—let us gaze upon them together.
At Nine Bends in Green Mountains lies Yǐngjìng Monastery; in the eighth month, the wind rises high over Pénlǐ Lake. At the tip of the staff, all is vividly clear;
one must know that though we share the same track, our paths are not the same.
When the Abbot returned to Hunan, he turned the *tathāgatagarbha* directly at its source.
When the wondrous timing is attained in daily life, moving freely in all directions—the Buddha’s hand has not yet been withdrawn, and the donkey’s feet have already been extended.
As soon as the thunder rolls, the lightning follows.
The Three Barriers are but empty talk; who can boast of the Elder Baoshang, who lived for a thousand years? From now on, when you meet people, do not treat them with levity;
in the south of Xiang and north of Tan, you must uphold [the Dharma] well.

Seeing off a monk returning to Fanyang to practice *dhyāna* and travel as a seeker is the duty of a man of spirit; his transformations should be like those of the Kun-fish of the Northern Sea. Have you not seen the Elder Yuanjue of our own province?
He bathes the Buddha-sun in light, dispelling the dust and darkness of the world.
The Lotus Sutra written in blood, a treasury upon treasury, rests upon a single hair-tip. Reveal it from that single hair-tip and behold it: more than sixty thousand words, drop by drop of blood;
this heart and liver cannot be cast even with gold.

To know one's parents' kindness by visiting them at their home, or to weave sandals to support them—these are not what is truly honored. What is the purpose of offering white gold to celebrate their longevity? Entrust this single phrase of gratitude to you:
it is when the red fruit ripens amidst the thorny forest.
Seeing off a monk returning to the ancient site of pure body and mind at Huaiqing: where else could one seek one’s hometown? The path by which he returns beneath Mount Pòtóu;
every tree’s autumnal sound accompanies the setting sun.
The one who seeks dhyāna returns easily to the world;
I dwell in bitterness amidst the entanglements of worldly affairs. The Master’s plans for returning are likewise many and busy. How can you reach the ground of no-mind?
We both love how the days are long in the empty mountains.
The monk Puhua goes through the marketplace shaking his bell; Lanchan plants taro by the edge of a cliff. The demeanor of these men of the Way is somewhat similar:
clad in coarse cloth, feigning madness, they return home.
The Abbot Fu returns to the Rulai Zang (Tathāgata-garbha) of Xiangjiang;
he alone permits the person of the present moment to grasp it intimately. Returning to Xiangjiang, do not abandon yourself;
held horizontally or used inverted, it is the family treasure in its entirety.
Fushun and I were fellow practitioners of old; you have sent me this from the south, so I shall open the seal. To present these from a thousand li away is like facing one another in person;
yet I regret that the flowers of the sky fall so profusely.
The boundary of the Venerable Vinaya Master returns to the numinous realm of Bai Zhang;
the celestial seeds of the Immortal Flower grow where the peach trees of the Imperial Garden bloom with spring within the caverns.
Having once been moistened by the rain and dew of the Nine Palaces, how could it endure even a speck of dust from the human world?
The monastic regulations of Baizhang for the forests of the world were established by the Master at the Imperial command to rectify the fundamental principles.
On the day the Dharma King’s decrees were once again put into practice, the dragon-elephants gathered in the assembly hall as the mallet was struck.
Inscribed upon the calligraphic masterpiece of Master Zhongfeng:
The karmic power of all Buddhas wells up like clouds poured from a jar; I am moved beyond measure to handle it, my tears falling in profusion.
Yet I fear the jade sheath of the Dragon-Slaying Sword— At the end, it will pierce through the roof and fly off with a clap of thunder.
Sending off Attendant Yun:
The ancestral tradition of our late master Zhu’an remains; the scenery of my old garden is still as it was. The bamboo staff—its avoidance and confrontation—is once more entrusted to you;
may it startle the divine dragon from its slumber in the ninefold abyss.
The arrowhead meets the target point-to-point; the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching seizes the opportune moment.
To employ this very function while remaining detached from it—observe the moment when a single shout deafens the ears.
The true attendant returns to Jiangxi to receive his formal training;
from Jiangxi he goes home to Fujian. A jade qilin gallops swiftly toward the celestial shore—do not let it become a fading-blossom apricot when you encounter its time;
you must see the spring beyond the kalpas of the peach of immortality.
The great capacity and great function of the Zen school are like shooting an arrow a hundred times with the expectation of hitting the mark each time.
When Niaokuo picked up a tuft of cloth and blew upon it, the weight in his wrist must have been no less than a thousand *jin*.

Sending forth the monk Zu’i together with the meaning of the teachings: how does one distinguish their similarities and differences? The profound gate passes through the bird-path; the Dharma-treasure is hidden in the dragon-palace.
The essence itself must be fully employed; when meeting the occasion, no effort is borrowed. When casually encountering a true master, do not begrudge the words spoken from east to west.

Seeing Master Wù depart from Samhan with his straw rain-hat upon his head, I dare not evade the journey southward in my inquiries. Not turning with the shifting of external objects, he prizes only the peace of his own mind.
Having passed through both the "Dharma-body verses" of Dushùn and the "Single-Character Barrier" of Yúnmén, he may now shake out his sleeves and return eastward.

Seeing that the gateways of the Master’s realization were distinct from those of others, I bid farewell to the Venerable Xin and set out on a journey of ten thousand li. Without the slightest slackening in body or mind, I have cultivated both wisdom and aspiration.

Shaking the bell and clapper to transform beings everywhere, I ride the iron ox through the Three Intersections. Spreading the sublime decree in the lands by the sea, the Great Dharma is destined to flow to the East.
In the same rhyme, I send off the monk:
The gateways of the various patriarchs are not easily exhausted. Amidst a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions, one must return to the source.

Deshan obtained only three years of life; Baizhang personally suffered deafness from a single shout. Do not vainly attempt to measure the ocean with an inch-long shell; do not cast a sharp sword into the air.
Vast space is one’s own field for resting; why need one insistently question the patriarch?
When serving as the abbot, he had the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* printed and distributed, with the title:
"The Celestial Wisdom Sun Shattering the Heavy Darkness. Respectfully reading his testament, one sees that his dignity encompasses the two polarities and clearly possesses the light.

The elephant’s transformation reached all species, wondrously leaving no trace; the fish, moved by his kindness, left behind pearls as a reward. Feeding the tiger, he sacrificed his body, and the stupa remains as a testament.
May he employ the Buddha-mind to proclaim the true teaching, and with humble loyalty seek to repay the grace of the Sacred Court.
As the Chief Seat Ding is sent forth, a million beings among humans and devas listen to the full presentation. The arrow meets the sharp point; it is not deployed in vain.

The *utpala* flower exists in the world of men, yet the great cooling tree is rare within the sight of eyes. At this place where he attains the seat and dons the robe, one must see him plow the field and seize the prize.
At the time of this meal: Be careful on the road ahead; you must exert yourself. The Nine Cauldrons of the Zen School hang by a single thread.
Following the verse of the late Master Gulin, I see off Chief Librarian Jing as he returns to his ancestral home at Taiping Temple to reside at the highest peak.
A single room is as if one were amidst ten thousand monks; it is like a lustrous pearl from the waters of Hepu.

Resplendent is the springtime of Lantian, where jade rings shimmer with brilliance. In the challenge, host and guest distinguish one another without a peer; in the Way, ruler and minister harmonize without borrowing merit.
The family reputation remains undiminished as it circles on; to follow in their footsteps, one must be equal to the ancients.
When the Venerable Da transcribed the Lotus Sūtra with his own blood, where the blood flowed and dripped, he applied needles and awls; forgetting both pain and endurance—who was this?

His valor surpassed that of Bhaiṣajyarāja when he burned his arm, and his swiftness exceeded that of the Dragon Girl when she offered her pearl. Thousand-petaled lotuses like layered clouds of brocade emerged, and a hundred-jeweled fragrant wind did not [cease].
Abiding in the blowing [of the wind], only then does this original intent begin to flourish. After two thousand years, one must well maintain this mindfulness.
As the Cloud Abbot returns to Huating, he is a *maṇi* jewel within the Tathāgata-garbha;
brought forth, it is fresh in every daily activity. The golden lock of the profound gate must be cast off.

Arms outstretched, one casts their body at will into the tiger’s den of Māra’s palace; only when a hundred rivers compete to flow together is it called the sea, and only when all things are impartial is it truly spring.
To display the oars and poles in the dance is the ultimate meaning; at the crossing of Zhu Jing, one encounters yet another person.
Chan Master Yinshou returned to Longhe Tianzhu in Hubei, where he repeatedly engaged in spiritual practice.
Great function is boundless, transcending both the orthodox and the deviant; with a single shout, one is captured seven times and released seven times.

Within these words lie the Three Essentials and the Three Mysteries. The guiding principles have already been revealed by the Venerable Master Chen, and his preaching of the Dharma was once heard at Dou.
Leading the heavens, he departed for Lake Mountain to establish the school's fundamental tenets. His eyes were clear as a rain of flowers fell before the green cliffs.
Joining the verse of Chan Master Hongzhi:
"The divine light of Donggu fills the great thousandfold world; the nine ridges wind and turn like a dragon asleep. Amidst the clouds, celestial music and robed immortals..."

Below, the wind and night, the *fùqú* and jade-drip clocks pass on. Who shall continue the brilliance of the True Lamp through successive generations? How much more pitiable is the kalpa-fire reaching as far as the Third Dhyāna Heaven!
My venerable grandfather conversed at the jade desk; one can imagine the monastic groves for two hundred years.

Master Maogong of the Cypress Courtyard once served as the recorder at Mount Zhongshan. He was invited to occupy the seat beside [the master] at Longhe, where the monastic community esteemed him for his maturity and experience.
When Scholar Shaoyan composed a verse in praise of him, I followed that rhyme to offer this gift to Zonggang:
Who could evaluate your resolve together with you? I admire your lofty spirit as you succeed the ancestral hall. You already resemble Master Lu returning to the snowy peaks.
Dong: How is it that Chuanshi was at Huating? At Tiantong, he remained seated before the Buddha; at the Precious Pagoda, he divided his body to listen to the sutras.
Furthermore, they made an appointment to build a hermitage together for the end of the year—a single green lamp amidst the night rain in the empty mountains.
The Dharma Master of Tianxi Town transcribed the Avataṃsaka Sūtra with his own blood;

at first, it startled one like the dim glow of the moon illuminating the night. Yet, one further perceives the springtime burgeoning within a cluster of brocade. The brilliant *uḍumbara* flowers are the blood from ten fingers;

the myriad layers of the Flower Treasury (*Kusumatalagarbha*) are but the point of a single needle. When facing the sun, he directly treads upon the crown of Vairocana—what need is there to hide his body in the north?
Within the Dipper, there fortunately exists the Changgan Pagoda, like a writing brush; from antiquity to the present, without interruption, it has inscribed upon the void.
Following the Pure Land poems of Master Zhongfeng:
Śākyamuni vowed to dwell in the five turbid worlds to subdue sentient beings and cause them to transcend [suffering]; Maitreya manifests in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

The lands [of the Buddhas] receive and guide beings to the stage of Buddhahood. They are like rain and dew on one hand, and frost and snow on the other; their nourishing moisture and their austere killing are each different.
Yet as Yin and Yang, cold and heat, operate through the four seasons, they equally effect the transformation of all things through generation and completion.
The vow-power of the Buddhas is likewise: pure lands and defiled lands are fundamentally one mind. They harmoniously encompass all lands throughout the ten directions, such that there is no duality.
Throughout the worlds of past, future, and present, within the pure ocean of the nature of sentient beings, even the slightest stir of a hair’s breadth becomes an obstruction;

thus they wander through the three realms, unaware of their home. How wearying it is that those sages and worthies have waited so long! How earnest is Zhongfeng’s exhortation to the world: like a traveler longing for home, or a child yearning for its kin.
Celestial music plays spontaneously and flowers rain down of their own accord; there, in the West, dwells that beautiful person.
Morning and evening, my thoughts are fixed upon this: for ten thousand years, a single thought lasts but a moment. When one thinks without thinking, subject and object are severed;

when one thinks without thinking, mind and境 (the objective world) are as they are. Sounds, scents, flavors, and touches enter into right concentration (*samāpatti*); seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing remain entirely as before.
In every land, the city of pure peace is perfectly realized; in every person, the immeasurable life is fully possessed.
Regarding the matter of sending this monk to the capital to practice Zen:
it is neither easy nor difficult. A fine steed does not wait for the whip; a sharp-eyed hawk will not eat the remains of a vulture’s meal.
With resolute determination, the Master has taken up his staff and come to the Three Kingdoms. Trusting his own feet, he has trampled across the Sea of Fragrant Water; turning his body, he leans—

The Diamond Mountains are overturned; the total functioning of the Great Utility appears and disappears at will. Before one’s eyes, the myriad phenomena are vast and empty. As summer approaches the Dragon River, he refuses to stay;
to advance further, one must surely rely on a hundred-foot pole. The Dharma assemblies of the masters of the capital are flourishing;

the pavilions and towers of the celestial palace open with sandalwood fragrance. Like thunder crashing and lightning flashing is the shout of Linji; like the heavens spinning and the earth turning is the barrier of Yunmen.
We look forward to meeting again to re-enter the chamber; drawing forth the "blow-piercing" sword, it makes one’s gall-bladder chill with fear.
Sending off the Jingci Secretary:

Those who can clearly manifest true nature and remain perpetually awakened without delusion are the Four Holy Ones (*ārya*). Within these holy ones, there are further gradations of distinction.

As he grew slightly older and entered the local school, his intelligence surpassed that of ordinary children; whenever he saw a character, he could immediately recite it from memory.
His parents personally took him out on excursions; whenever they reached a Buddhist temple, he would invariably pay his respects with such deep devotion that he could not bear to leave.
