Below Mount Huáng, the disciples secretly went to Mount Jīnhuá to convey the sentiments of the former residents of the temple, Rǔjié and Jǐngcāo, to Míng, saying:
"Our late master succeeded in flourishing the ancestral Way and served as a model for humans and devas; he was fully in accord with the heart of the Emperor."
Having been graced by the imperial favor, it is fitting that there be a record to show future generations.

As I have served in the office of the Grand Historian and was honored to be a friend of the late Master, who else is more suitable than I to compose this inscription? I venture to request it based on the memorial presented by my fellow disciple Tingjun.
When I recall that when the Master passed away, I traveled from no less than a thousand *li* away to bring my own robes and articles of use as tokens of my eternal remembrance.
Farewell. If there are those who look toward Ming for guidance, it would be improper for me to excuse myself on the grounds of declining health.
I have carefully examined the records: His Excellency’s name was Dayin, his courtesy name Xiaoyin. He belonged to the Chen clan, descendants of Chen Cao, a Minister of State during the Tang dynasty.

His family had resided in Jiangzhou for generations, later migrating to Nanchang; thus, he is now a native of Nanchang in Longxing. From childhood, His Excellency was open-minded and bright; as soon as he was taught the classics, he...

He mastered the recitation [of the scriptures]. At seven years of age, he frequented the monasteries; whenever he beheld a Buddhist image, he would immediately prostrate himself, gazing upon it with such longing that he forgot to return home.

His parents, knowing they could not keep him there, allowed him to leave the household at nine. He went to rely on his uncle, Master Yunshang, at the Shuili (Water-Land) Monastery in his native prefecture and received the tonsure.
He took Master Zhang, a disciple of Yunshang, as his preceptor. Soon thereafter, at the age of seventeen, he received full ordination. At first...

He arrived at Mount Lu and paid his respects to Master Wansong Xingxiu of Kaixian, remaining there to serve as the internal secretary (*neiji*). Subsequently, he was sent to Baiyang Mountain to attend upon Chan Master Huiji Xi.
Upon their first meeting, the Master held him in high esteem and treated him with great respect. From the position of internal secretary, he was promoted to the office of the record-keeper (*jishi*).
One day he questioned him, saying, "Huanglong received the essential meaning at Letan and led his disciples to travel through the mountains, establishing monasteries.

Yet when he saw Ciming, his spirit was drained and sweat poured from him. Where did his fault lie? The Master [Dongshan] shouted back, "What are you looking for—an old kernel inside a thousand-year-old peach pit?
The Teacher [Xuedou] marveled at this even more. On another day, he questioned him with the story of Baizhang and the wild fox.
The Master said: "Tell me, how is it that by not falling into cause and effect one falls into the body of a wild fox, yet by not being ignorant of cause and effect one sheds the body of a wild fox?
Wherein lies the point of benefit or harm? As the official was about to answer, the Master suddenly shouted at him.

From that moment on, the official’s lifelong stagnation was completely dissolved like ice melting. The official often remarked: "As the former masters have said, as long as there is even the slightest doubt, one has not reached the state of non-attainment."

How could he, who had mastered the teachings so as to move with ease in every direction, fail to further investigate the scriptural canons? He also extensively studied the doctrines of the Confucianists, the Daoists, and the various schools of thought.
When his master moved to Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou, he was appointed as the First Seat (Dìyīzuò), but he declined and did not accept; instead, he remained in the position of Secretary (Jìshì).

Later, he emerged from seclusion to reside at Wuhui on Lake Dongting, where he offered the fragrant incense of his devotion to become his master’s Dharma heir. After serving for three years, he departed.

He traveled through the regions of Jiang and Zhe, later returning to Jingci Monastery. At that time, many eminent masters who were his seniors in the Dharma all became lifelong friends with him, disregarding their differences in age.
He once visited Master Zhongfeng Ben on Mount Tianmu; they sat in conversation until midnight when a great wind arose with such force it seemed it would tear the cliff rocks asunder.
Everyone around him was struck with terror and recoiled, yet he remained unmoved. Zhongfeng held him in the highest esteem and regarded him as extraordinary.

At Fenghuangshan Daboguo Temple, the monastery had been destroyed by disaster and its dharma seat was temporarily vacant. The Xingzhangyuan (Office for Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs) relied upon the Master to restore the ruins.
Once the Master arrived, the buildings were entirely renewed, and the regulations became more magnificent than before.
As for the land that had been seized by powerful commoners, he reclaimed it all and returned it [to the temple]. [This was done under the auspices of] Chancellor Tughan Temür.
Lord Han presided over the affairs of the Circuit Court (Xingyuan). Being well-acquainted with the Master, he appointed him as the Abbot of Central India (Zhong Tianzhu).

At that time, the temple had been destroyed by fire; yet within less than a year, it was entirely restored to its former state. In the first year of the Tianli era, an imperial edict was issued to establish the former residence in Jinling as the Great Longxiang Jiqing Temple.
A master of renowned virtue was sought out to serve as its founding abbot, and the Master was the first to be selected for this honor. The following year...

He was specially conferred with the third rank of the *wénjiē* (literary grade) to serve as the prefix for his Dharma name. Furthermore, the following year, he was summoned by imperial decree to the capital.

Upon entering the Quanzhang Pavilion for an audience, he was granted a seat. After a long while, the Emperor inquired about the essentials of the Dharma; his responses were in accord with the Imperial will.
When the matter of his spiritual lineage was raised, the Attendant Scholar of Calligraphy, the Duke Yu Jí, received an edict to compose a stupa inscription for Huījī. This having been done, moreover—
He renamed the Zhong Tianzhu Temple, inscribing its plaque with the characters "Tianli Yongzu" (Perpetual Blessings of the Celestial Calendar) to commemorate the Master’s merit in restoring it.
Furthermore, he had the official Yu write the inscriptions for the Master’s private hermitage, which was named "Guangzhi" (Extensive Wisdom).

The gifts bestowed upon him—including a sable fur robe, a golden patchwork robe, and other precious articles of clothing and use—were all marks of exceptional favor; even his attendants were granted such honors in advance.

An imperial messenger was dispatched to convey the decree, and he was accommodated at the Taixi Zongyin Yuan. By imperial order, sumptuous meals were provided for the śramaṇas, and he remained there for ten days.

The Emperor’s inquiries after his welfare were most thorough. He was summoned for an audience once more, after which he took his leave to return home; the ceremonies for his farewell were exceedingly generous.

After the Duke had returned south, the Emperor again dispatched an envoy with an imperial edict to bestow his protection; there was not a single month that passed without the distribution of incense and ceremonial silk.

When His Majesty ascended the throne, the honors accorded to him became even more magnificent. An imperial decree was issued ordering Dehui of Baizhang Mountain to recompile the *Chanyuan Qinggui* (Pure Rules of the Chan Forest), and the Duke was further charged with its collation.
He subsequently established it in nine chapters. Once the work was completed, all quarters of the realm took it as their model. The Duke—
Whenever he addressed the assembly, he would cite the story of Baizhang and the wild fox, saying: "Baizhang’s wild fox; the wild fox, Baizhang.
Buried in one pit. May you rest in peace. He remained in this position for eight years without being permitted to take leave, and then stayed for another nine years.
On the day before his passing, he went to bid farewell to the Grand Minister of the Censorate, Duke Tuohan, as well as several acquaintances, engaging them in cordial conversation.
It was the end of the day, approaching the time for his passing. Yet he remained seated in the lotus posture despite his failing strength.
He entrusted his disciples with the gold and silk bestowed upon him as rewards, instructing them to build a Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall to repay the grace of the state; he had no other concerns.
He then composed a verse and passed away at the age of sixty-one (the forty-sixth year of the Xia calendar). He ordained several disciples, who attained the Dharma and lived separately.
There were several dozen monasteries [visited by him]. There are records of his discourses from four assemblies. His external collection is titled the *Pūshí jí* (The Pū Collection).

Because his mother was advanced in years and he was unable to attend to her through regular visits and inquiries, he often said to himself that he felt ashamed when compared to Muzhou, who wove pū grass to serve his parents.
Consequently, he named his study "Pū" and used that name for his collection. As for the writings he produced, they lacked the withered stillness of mountain forests.

His demeanor shifted through various transformations, opening and closing with a brilliance that dazzled the eyes; his discourse was grand and磊落 (lofty and resolute), emerging entirely from the correct path, never once succumbing to partiality or obscuration.

The Duke of Yu praised him as being like the wilds of Dongting, where all the musical instruments play together—resounding and majestic, causing dragons and serpents to leap forth and strange creatures to flee in terror, while a profound inspiration is stirred within.
As for the principles of the Name-Teachings (Confucian ethics) and the integrity of moral conduct, he was likewise exemplary.

His feelings were stirred and his spirit roused with such vigor that even those long experienced in letters could not surpass him; people considered him one who truly understood the essence of discourse.
Initially, Zhao Gong Mengfu of the Wei State had not yet met the Master, but upon obtaining his writings, he praised them incessantly and immediately ordered his carriage to visit him.
At that time, worthy scholars and gentlemen all admired him and sought his friendship. His physical presence was imposing and distinguished, and his character was as open and expansive as the sky.
Even during the intense cold of midwinter, he would have a person carry a woolen robe; whenever he encountered an orphan or a destitute person on the road, he would immediately cast it to them.
He did not allow people to know his name or surname. When others were ill, he gave them medicine; when they died, he provided them with coffins.
His treatment of others was such as this, yet he lived frugally for himself. He wore a single patched robe that he would not change for several decades. His biography states:

there was a massive camphor tree at his ancestral tomb, and a diviner said, "When this tree withers, a famous monk shall appear. When the Master was born, the tree indeed withered. Furthermore, during his life, his house...

All were moved with awe. His father had passed away early, and his mother was still in the prime of her youth; she immediately observed the fasts and practiced the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi), whereby a white lotus flower miraculously sprang from the earth.
In that same year, the Master resided at Baoguo Temple. On the day he entered parinirvāṇa, there was a great storm of wind and rain.
On the day of the encoffining, dense clouds gathered from all sides and a chilling wind blew with solemnity.
On the day of the interment, it rained in the southeast of the city, yet the western part alone remained entirely dry. These traces of spiritual anomaly can be verified and are not false.
That his life met such a prosperous era, beginning in glory and ending in sorrow, was surely no mere coincidence. The inscription says:
Formerly, under the previous sovereign, while the Dragon lay hidden in the lower realms, his secluded dwelling was transformed into a sacred sanctuary.
The fourfold assembly of devas and humans gathered like rushing rivers and clustering clouds; the gateway to liberation was majestic, and you served as its great pillars and beams.
In this most august and prosperous age, the Golden Wheel Ruler governs the world; he has shown favor to his old friends, and envoys arrive from every direction.
Incense was presented in a casket to manifest sincerity, and the great decree was proclaimed: "By means of the Five Mountains, all shall be brought under your governance.
Regarding all matters of the Śākya teachings, you are to be the presiding master. Seek out the lost models of the past and employ them to continue the glorious light of your ancestors' benevolence.
Your robes shall cover you with honor surpassing even the dragon-embroidered ceremonial vestments. Were it not for one of public standing and long-standing virtue, who could bear such a burden?"
Where the principles of the classics remain, what has fallen must be raised up; the wooden clapper sounds once more, establishing the model again and again with perfect symmetry.
Directly pointing and singularly upholding, he set forth the correct beginning and end; erecting the banner of the Dharma, he acted as a great refuge.

Secretly assisting the supreme transformation, he was like a timely rain for all things. How could he not have spared us? When the news of his passing reached the imperial throne, the Emperor stood in the courtyard of the palace in mourning.
Upon the Ridge of Stone, Lofty rises this stūpa; The historian carves this inscription, To perpetuate its glory for ten thousand ages.
